title: 第六章辛十四娘第七章尸变第八章 画壁
lines: 第六章辛十四娘
广平府有个书生，叫冯子平。
他家境殷实，父母早亡，留下几十亩薄田和一座宅院。冯子平不爱读书，不爱经营，唯独爱喝酒。一天三顿，顿顿不离酒，喝醉了就躺在院子里看天，看得眼睛发直，嘴里嘀嘀咕咕的，不知道说些什么。邻居们都说，冯家这小子，算是废了。
冯子平不在乎。他爹娘死得早，没人管他，他想怎么活就怎么活。
这天傍晚，冯子平又喝醉了。他晃晃悠悠地走出家门，往村外走。走到一处荒坡上，看见一座小庙。庙不大，只有一间正殿，殿门开着，里面供着一尊神像，看不清是谁。庙前站着一个女子，穿着红色衣裙，梳着高高的发髻，背对着他。
夕阳照在她身上，那红衣像一团火，烧得冯子平眼睛发直。他酒劲上来，走上前去，伸手拍了拍那女子的肩膀。
“姑娘，你一个人在这儿做什么？”
那女子转过身来。冯子平的手僵在半空。酒，一瞬间醒了一半。
女子十五六岁的样子，眉目如画，肤若凝脂，一双眼睛又黑又亮，像两颗浸在溪水里的黑石子。她看着冯子平，没有害怕，也没有恼怒，只是微微皱了皱眉。那种神情不是嫌弃，是——怎么说呢，像是一个人看见地上爬过一只蚂蚁，不讨厌，但也不会放在心上。
“你喝醉了。”她说。声音很淡，像山风穿过竹林。
“我没醉。”冯子平说，“姑娘，你叫什么名字？”
女子没有回答。她转身走进庙里，关上了门。
冯子平站在门外，愣了很久。他拍了拍门，没人应。他又拍了几下，还是没人应。他在庙门口坐了一会儿，酒全醒了，觉得有些冷，便起身回家了。
冯子平不知道，那女子叫辛十四娘，是狐仙。
她修行了八百年，离成仙只差一步。她的功德簿上，写满了八百年来做的善事——救人、助人、渡人。但那些功德，都是“无心”的。她救人是因为想救，帮人是因为该帮，做完就忘了，从不记在心上。无心为善，虽善不赏。她的功德够了，但天书不认。她需要做一件“有心”的善事——一件她知道自己在做善事、做了之后会记在心里的善事。
这一步，她在人间等了三百年，一直没有等到。
她不知道，这一步快到了。
那天夜里，冯子平没有睡。他躺在床上，翻来覆去，脑子里全是那双眼睛。第二天一早，他又去了那座庙。庙门开着，里面空空的，什么都没有。他在庙里庙外找了一圈，连个人影都没看见。
他以为自己是喝醉了做的梦。但他心里清楚，那不是梦。
他连着去了半个月，每天都去，从早等到晚。第十五天傍晚，那女子又出现了。她站在庙门口，手里拿着一枝野花，低头闻着。听见脚步声，抬起头，看见冯子平，又皱了皱眉。
“你怎么又来了？”
“等你。”冯子平说。
“等我做什么？”
“我想娶你。”
十四娘看着他，看了很久。这个人，长得不好看，穿得不体面，满身酒气，说话冒失。但他是认真的。他的眼睛是干净的，没有算计，没有贪念，就是单纯地——想要她。
“你不怕我？”她问。
“怕你什么？”
“怕我不是人。”
冯子平愣了一下，然后笑了。“你是人也好，不是人也罢，我都要娶你。”
十四娘没有说话。她活了八百年，见过无数人，听过无数话。但这么直白的，还是头一回。她忽然想：也许，这就是她的“有心”之缘。不是她选他，是天送来的。
“好。”她说。
辛十四娘嫁给了冯子平。
消息传出去，半个广平府都炸了。冯子平？那个酒鬼？那个败家子？那个连秀才都没考上的废物？他凭什么？凭他命好？凭他祖上积德？凭他喝醉了在荒坡上撞大运？
冯子平不在乎。他高兴得像做梦一样。他问十四娘为什么嫁他，十四娘说：“看你顺眼。”他信了。他什么都信。她说什么他都信。
婚后的日子，平平淡淡。十四娘不爱说话，不爱笑，每天早起扫地、洗衣、做饭、织布。她做得好，但做得慢。每做一件事，她都要想一想——这件事该怎么做？为什么要这么做？做完了，别人会不会高兴？
她以前在山里修行，从不用想这些。现在她要想一个人的心思，要猜一个人高不高兴，要在一个人身边活着。她觉得很累。但累里有一点点甜。
冯子平对她好。他没什么钱，但会把最好的东西留给她。他没什么本事，但会在她累了的时候给她倒杯水。他没什么出息，但会在喝醉了之后拉着她的手说：“十四娘，你是我这辈子见过的最好的人。”
十四娘看着他，心里有一个地方软了一下。她不知道那是什么。她以为是习惯，是怜悯，是她修行八百年积累的慈悲心。
她不知道，那是种子。埋在地下，还没发芽。

Chapter 6 Xin Si Niang
There was a scholar in Guangping Mansion named Feng Ziping.
His family was well off, his parents died young, leaving behind dozens of acres of thin farmland and a house. Feng Ziping doesn't like studying or running a business, but he only likes drinking. He drank three meals a day and drank every meal. When he was drunk, he would lie in the yard and watch the sky. His eyes would stare straight at the sky and he would mumble, not knowing what to say. Neighbors all said that this boy from the Feng family was considered useless.
Feng Ziping didn't care. His parents died early, and no one cared about him. He could live however he wanted.
That evening, Feng Ziping got drunk again. He staggered out of the house and walked out of the village. Walking to a deserted slope, I saw a small temple. The temple is not big, with only one main hall. The door of the hall is open, and there is a statue of a god inside. It is not clear who it is. There was a woman standing in front of the temple, wearing a red dress and combing her hair in a high bun, with her back to him.
The setting sun shone on her body, and the red dress was like a ball of fire, burning Feng Ziping's eyes straight. He got drunker, walked forward, reached out and patted the woman on the shoulder.
"Girl, what are you doing here alone?"
The woman turned around. Feng Ziping's hands froze in mid-air. The wine made me half awake in an instant.
The woman looks about fifteen or sixteen years old, with picturesque features, smooth skin, and a pair of eyes as dark and bright as two black pebbles immersed in a stream. She looked at Feng Ziping, not afraid or angry, but frowned slightly. That look wasn't disgust, it was - how should I put it, like a person who sees an ant crawling on the ground and doesn't hate it, but doesn't take it to heart either.
"You're drunk," she said. The sound was very light, like the mountain wind passing through the bamboo forest.
"I'm not drunk." Feng Ziping said, "Girl, what's your name?"
The woman didn't answer. She turned and walked into the temple and closed the door.
Feng Ziping stood outside the door, stunned for a long time. He knocked on the door, but no one answered. He patted a few more times, but still no one responded. He sat at the door of the temple for a while, sobered up from the wine and felt a little cold, so he got up and went home.
Feng Ziping didn't know that the woman's name was Xin Shisi Niang, a fox fairy.
She has been practicing for eight hundred years and is only one step away from becoming an immortal. Her merit book is filled with good deeds she has done over the past eight hundred years - saving, helping, and helping others. But those merits are all "unintentional". She saves people because she wants to save them, helps people because she needs to help them, and then forgets them after she does them, never remembering them in her heart. Doing good deeds unintentionally will not reward you even if you do good deeds. Her merits are sufficient, but the Book of Heaven does not recognize her. She needs to do a good deed that is “intentional”—a good deed that she knows she is doing and will remember after she does it.
She has been waiting for this step for three hundred years in the human world, but she has not waited for it.
She didn't know that this step was coming soon.
That night, Feng Ziping didn't sleep. He lay on the bed, tossing and turning, and all he could think about was those eyes. Early the next morning, he went to the temple again. The temple door was open, but it was empty, with nothing inside. He looked around inside and outside the temple, but didn't see even a single figure.
He thought he was drunk and dreaming. But he knew in his heart that it was not a dream.
He went there for half a month, every day, from morning until night. On the evening of the fifteenth day, the woman appeared again. She stood at the door of the temple, holding a wild flower in her hand and lowering her head to smell it. Hearing footsteps, he raised his head and frowned again when he saw Feng Ziping.
"Why are you here again?"
"Waiting for you." Feng Ziping said.
"What are you waiting for me to do?"
"I want to marry you."
The fourteenth mother looked at him for a long time. This man was not good-looking, dressed in a disgraceful way, smelled of alcohol, and spoke rashly. But he means it. His eyes were clean, without calculation or greed, he just simply wanted her.
"Aren't you afraid of me?" she asked.
"What are you afraid of?"
"I'm afraid I'm not human."
Feng Ziping was stunned for a moment, and then smiled. "Whether you are a human being or not, I will marry you."
The fourteenth mother said nothing. She has lived for eight hundred years, met countless people, and heard countless things. But this is the first time it has been so straightforward. She suddenly thought: Maybe, this is her "intention". She didn't choose him, he was sent by God.
"Okay." she said.
Xin Shisi Niang married Feng Ziping.
When the news spread, half of Guangping Mansion exploded. Feng Ziping? That drunkard? That prodigal? That loser who didn't even pass the exam? Why should he? Depends on his life? Based on the virtues accumulated by his ancestors? How could he get lucky on a deserted slope when he was drunk?
Feng Ziping didn't care. He was as happy as in a dream. He asked the Fourteenth Niang why she married him, and the Fourteenth Niang said, "It pleases you." He believed it. He believes everything. He believed whatever she said.
The days after marriage are ordinary. The fourteenth mother doesn't like to talk or laugh. She gets up early every day to sweep the floor, do laundry, cook, and weave. She does it well, but slowly. Every time she did something, she had to think about it—how to do it? Why do this? Once it’s done, will others be happy?
She used to practice in the mountains and never had to think about this. Now she wants to think about someone's thoughts, guess whether someone is happy or not, and live by someone's side. She felt very tired. But there is a little bit of sweetness in the tiredness.
Feng Ziping was kind to her. He doesn't have much money, but he will leave the best things to her. He has no skills, but he will give her a glass of water when she is tired. He has no future, but he will hold her hand when he is drunk and say: "Sissi, you are the best person I have ever seen in my life."
The Fourteenth Mother looked at him and felt a little soft in her heart. She didn't know what it was. She thought it was habit, compassion, the compassion she had accumulated through eight hundred years of practice.
She didn't know it was a seed. Buried in the ground, it has not sprouted yet.
